prompt: Human: Do you have any tips on how to stay safe during a heatwave?
response:
Yes, sure! It really can be quite hazardous in certain circumstances, and it’s important to be aware of your own risks. There are some general tips to help cope with a heat wave:

Stay Hydrated, and Avoid Hot Spots

Drink plenty of water every day to stay hydrated, and don’t let your bladder run dry. During the heat of a heatwave, your circulatory system works harder to keep your muscles warm, and this can put a strain on your kidneys. So it’s a good idea to have some non-sticky drinks on hand, like water, coconut water or fresh juice in cooler bottles, to keep you hydrated, but not too sweet.

Stay in the Shade

Going out into the sun can be toxic, so it’s best to minimize exposure to the sun whenever possible. If you have to be outside, try to find a shaded spot, or try and stand with your back to a building or an overhanging tree or bush, and have a scarf, hat, or sunglasses on to protect yourself from the sun’s rays.

Also Take Care of Your Skin and Hair

During a heatwave, your skin is more sensitive to the sun’s rays, so it’s a good idea to protect your skin, and you’ll want to keep your hair moisturized too, if you have dry skin or hair.

Take Breaks in the Cool Air

The air will be drier in a heatwave, so try to take as many “cool air” breaks as you can, whenever you’re outdoors, so you won’t get too hot. This means taking a walk around the block or going for a short walk to the park, or having the air conditioning set to an easily adjustable level and taking a short cool shower to refresh yourself.

Eat Your Vegetables and Fruit

Heatwaves are a great time to eat lots of fresh vegetables and fruit, as they’re often at their peak in a heatwave, and are naturally lower in sugar.

Take Enough Time to Relax

If you’re feeling tired or achy, take a longer break in the cool air and rest. If you can still do an outdoor activity, like walking, you’ll be happier and feel better in the end.

Stay Cool in a Home

Try to keep temperatures in your home somewhat lower than outside, by moving in and out of air-conditioned rooms. You could also have some air-filters and/or air-Conditioning units in your home, to help keep the air cooler. But air-conditioning isn’t often appropriate during a heatwave, so watch out for other ways to combat the heat, like turning on fans.

Take Enough Time to Eat Outside

Don’t rush through the meal while the sun’s out, as this can make you feel tired and dehydrated, and it means you won’t end up eating as much. So if you’re planning on eating outside, either at a park or somewhere else in the open air, plan your route and set up your picnic in a shaded spot first, if possible.

Avoid Hot Drinks

Don’t get into the habit of drinking hot drinks in a heatwave, as this can make you feel hot and stuffy, and it can increase your chances of getting a fever, which can be harmful if it rises above 102 degrees Fahrenheit. If you have to drink something hot, try a hot herbal tea with honey, instead of hot chocolate, or hot water with lemon and honey.

Keep Calm

For some people, especially the elderly and those who’ve been sick before, heatwaves can be extremely uncomfortable and distressing. But if you feel yourself feeling tired, moody, or stressed, take a break and do something you enjoy, or get out of the sun and take some time for yourself in a fresh environment, like a cool bath, on a comfortable bed, or even a nap if you can.

Avoid Hot Weather by Walking

If you need to move, try to do so on foot, in the early morning or the late evening, rather than in the middle of the day.

Use Shades on the House

Put up blinds or curtains that can still let in light, if you need to use them, and make sure these can be easily opened and closed.

Keep the Air Clean

If you’re going to be outside in a heatwave, try to avoid areas with high concentrations of pollution, like traffic and industrial areas, because these can be especially hot and stuffy. Also, to avoid breathing in some of the chemicals in the air, try to avoid areas near airports.

Use Air Conditioners Sparingly

Remember, air-conditioners cost money and do a lot of work to cool an air-conditioned room, so use them sparingly, in cases of extreme heat or when it’s necessary to keep a room cool. In summer, it’s preferable to use natural and low-tech ways to keep air cool, like walking in the air over a body of water (a lake, river, pond or river bed).

Ask for Indefinite Cold Bath and Hot Bath

If you need a hot bath to cool yourself, ask for a short one. You can also take an indefinite cold bath, where you’ll soak in cool water for five to ten minutes. This can be helpful to get some relief from hot and stuffy feeling.

Take Heat-Breaks

When you feel really hot and need to take a break, go outdoors for a while and take a cool shower or bath. You’ll also have a chance to enjoy yourself outside, and this can help reduce fatigue and make you feel less hot.

Don’t Be Afraid to Ask for Help

Heatwaves are dangerous, so don’t hesitate to ask for help if you need it. If you know someone who’s getting very hot under the sun, go get a glass of water for them right away.

Also, if you see someone who might need help in the heat, like an elderly person or someone with a disability, you should ask them if they need help, and get them to sit down, and let them make themselves comfortable in a cool place.
